The narrative audit, in practice¶

A worked companion to Auditing the narrative — disciplined measurement of how discourse changes¶

Corpus accounts of how meaning and terminology change are easy to produce and hard to falsify. The same flexible pipeline — choose the terms, the windows, the comparison, the test — can be steered, usually with no intent to deceive, toward almost any expected story. The narrative-audit pattern answers this not with a new statistic but with a discipline imposed around whatever method the question calls for: predictions committed in advance (including ones designed to fail), null and placebo controls on every headline claim, a safeguard against the polysemy trap, and a standing preference for converging evidence over any single number.

This notebook walks that discipline end to end, across the corpora we studied, organized by the questions an audit asks. At each step the point is not only which instrument answers the question but what control makes the answer auditable. It is meant to read as an argument, and to serve as the skeleton for the paper. One theme recurs — and it is the paper's as well: the most persuasive results here are the ones that failed.

§ The audit asks… Instrument(s) Discipline on display Corpus
1 What vocabulary marks a frame — really? keyness (+ volcano/bars) null control + confound matching Hansard immigration framing
2 Richer vocabulary, or just bigger? Hill numbers + rarefaction the size-fair control Asylum: Con vs Lab
3 What does a term travel with? collocation_shift · network convergent corroboration Hansard framing
4 When did it change — where predicted? trajectory + seven detectors placebo / anchor logic Asylum: "illegal" @ Brexit
5 Which competing term won? succession (S-curve + concentration) prediction + falsifier, cause cross-check NYT race relay
6 Real change, or noise? S-curve vs FIT vs Kalman vs PK/PD honest negatives, converging evidence NYT immigration
7 Did the meaning change — right sense? semantic family + sense_drift + the polysemy trap the polysemy safeguard Hansard + CBD (PubMed & Twitter)
8 Is it one language, or four? keyness as a language-identity probe validation + two-wolves, on non-English Croatian vs Serbian (SETIMES)
9 Does drift travel to another language? succession + diffusion S-curves a documented 100-yr reform Turkish (Turkronicles 1920–2024)

The stance: commit first, let the corpus adjudicate¶

Before retrieving a single document, the audit writes down — for each claimed shift — a directional prediction, an explicit falsifier, and, where the logic of the change licenses it, a negative prediction: a place the shift should not occur. Several studies below were staked as adversarial two-wolves bets — a left-leaning and a right-leaning reading registered in advance, the corpus left to decide between them.

Negative predictions are the load-bearing move. A scoreboard on which everything passes is uninformative: a sufficiently flexible pipeline can make anything pass. A scoreboard that includes predictions designed to fail, and which then fail as predicted, shows the registration was binding. Several of the project's narrative studies were staked this way as adversarial two-wolves bets — a left-leaning and a right-leaning reading committed in advance, the corpus left to decide.

A note on what this notebook is. The strongest, independently timestamped registration lives in the paper; this notebook is a walkthrough of the instruments and the controls that make their outputs auditable, on the corpora we studied. Read it for the discipline applied to each tool, not as the registered demonstration itself.

In [1]:
import os, sys, warnings
os.environ.setdefault('HF_HUB_OFFLINE', '1')   # use the local sentence-transformer cache
sys.path.insert(0, '../build')
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, pycorpdiff as pcd
from IPython.display import Image, display
pd.set_option('display.width', 150)

ASYLUM = Path('/Users/jasonturner/Projects/pycorpdiff/examples/_cache/hansard_asylum_2010_2023.parquet')
STOP = set('the of to and a in that is for on it as be by with are was this we i you he '
           'his her our their not have has had will would can could but or if so an at'.split())
EMB = pcd.SBERTEmbedder()   # real sentence-transformer (all-MiniLM-L6-v2), from local cache

hansard = pcd.load_hansard_sample()
imm = hansard.slice(topic='immigration')
human, criminal = imm.slice(frame='humanising'), imm.slice(frame='criminalising')
_adf = pd.read_parquet(ASYLUM); _adf['year'] = _adf['date'].dt.year
asylum = pcd.from_dataframe(_adf, text_col='text', meta_cols=('date','year','house','party_abbrev'))
print(f'loaded: hansard sample (immigration: {len(human)}+{len(criminal)} speeches) + '
      f'{len(asylum):,}-doc asylum corpus')

loaded: hansard sample (immigration: 28+21 speeches) + 10,124-doc asylum corpus

1. What vocabulary marks a frame — and is the marking real?¶

The audit's first question is the oldest in corpus linguistics: which words separate two bodies of text? keyness (the log-likelihood ratio) answers it. But the answer is treacherous — "language is never, ever random," so a keyness list always finds something, and the items a reader picks off it are hostage to corpus composition and a handful of high-leverage documents. So the question is really two: what separates the frames, and does the separation survive scrutiny? We ask both of the humanising vs criminalising framings of immigration, and let the audit's two controls — a null and a confound check — do the disciplining.

1a · Raw keyness — the volcano and the ranked bars¶

In [2]:
K = pcd.compare(human, criminal).keyness(min_count=5)
display(K.plot().properties(width=560, height=300, title='Keyness volcano: humanising (+) vs criminalising (−)'))
K.plot(kind='bar', n=14).properties(width=520, title='Top terms by signed G²')

1c · Confound control — does the signal survive matching on year?¶

In [4]:
def top_content(kt, n=8):
    t = kt.table[~kt.table['term'].isin(STOP)].head(n)
    return t[['term', 'log_ratio', 'g2']].reset_index(drop=True)

m = pcd.match(human, criminal, on=['year'], seed=0)
matched = pcd.compare(m.a_matched, m.b_matched).keyness(min_count=5)
print('RAW (humanising + / criminalising −):'); print(top_content(K).to_string(index=False))
print('\nCEM-MATCHED on year:'); print(top_content(matched).to_string(index=False))

What the audit added. The volcano and bars make the raw effect legible; the permutation null answers "keyness always finds something" by sitting the observed statistic against a shuffled-label distribution; and matching answers the confound — watch the dramatic frame words (criminal, gangs, invasion) attenuate sharply once the slices are balanced on year, a warning that the raw list rode partly on when each frame was used. Explore with raw keyness; claim only what survives the null and the match. (The reference baseline reframes the question entirely: what is special about this discourse versus ordinary English.)

2. A confound hiding in plain sight — richer vocabulary, or just bigger?¶

The same rule — control the obvious confound before you claim — recurs in a place that catches many studies: corpus size. A larger corpus looks more varied for no reason but its length. The instrument here is borrowed from ecology, and it is the diversity analogue of §1's matching.

In [6]:
from pycorpdiff.lexical import hill_numbers, rarefaction
commons = asylum.slice(house='Commons')
con, lab = commons.slice(party_abbrev='Con'), commons.slice(party_abbrev='Lab')
print('Within-corpus, length-corrected (lexical_diversity):')
print('  Con:', pcd.lexical_diversity(con).summary())
print('  Lab:', pcd.lexical_diversity(lab).summary())
vcon, vlab = con.vocab().values, lab.vocab().values
n = min(int(vcon.sum()), int(vlab.sum()))
display(pd.DataFrame({
    'party': ['Conservative', 'Labour'], 'tokens': [int(vcon.sum()), int(vlab.sum())],
    'richness q0': [hill_numbers(vcon, 0), hill_numbers(vlab, 0)],
    'expShannon q1': [round(hill_numbers(vcon, 1), 1), round(hill_numbers(vlab, 1), 1)],
    'invSimpson q2': [round(hill_numbers(vcon, 2), 1), round(hill_numbers(vlab, 2), 1)],
    f'rarefied richness @ {n:,}': [round(rarefaction(vcon, n), 1), round(rarefaction(vlab, n), 1)]}))

  Lab: LexicalDiversityResult(label="house='Commons', party_abbrev='Lab'", |tokens|=936,804, |types|=19,650, TTR=0.021, MATTR=0.708, MTLD=86.7, HD-D=36.31)

What the audit added. Naively Conservative looks at least as rich — it has more tokens. But it uses fewer types, and rarefying both parties to a common size widens Labour's lead: volume was masking the difference, not creating it. Length-corrected lexical_diversity answers the within-corpus question; rarefaction is the size-fair control for any cross-corpus comparison — exactly the move matching made in §1, in a different currency.

3. Meaning travels in company — beyond the single word¶

Keyness ranks words in isolation, but framing often lives in pairings: who a word stands next to. Two instruments widen the lens — collocation_shift for one term's changing company, cooccurrence_network for the whole relational field. Their value to the audit is convergence: a second, structurally different instrument that corroborates §1 rather than re-running it.

3a · Collocation shift — which companions of 'immigrant' differ by frame?¶

In [7]:

display(cs.plot(n=12).properties(width=520, title="Collocates of 'immigrant': humanising vs criminalising"))
cs.table.head(8)

3b · Co-occurrence network — the discourse as a graph¶

In [8]:
net = pcd.cooccurrence_network(imm, top_n=18, window=5, measure='PMI', min_count=4, min_cooccur=4)
print(net.summary())
net.plot(width=640, height=480, max_edges=28, label_top_n=18)

NetworkResult(measure=PMI, window=5, nodes=18, edges=82)
Out[8]:

What the audit added. The collocates of immigrant split cleanly by frame — criminal, gangs, threat on one side, family, worker, community on the other — corroborating §1 from a different statistic (convergence, not a second bite at the same one). The network zooms out to the relational structure. Reach for these when the unit of meaning is a pairing or a cluster, not a lone term.

4. When did usage change — and did it change where you said it would?¶

Now the temporal core, and the audit's third control: the placebo. For a change pinned to a dated event, an honest test must distinguish an effect that appears only at the anchor you committed to from one the time-series machinery would manufacture anywhere. Seven instruments answer different flavours of "did it change?" on one quarterly trajectory — illegal in asylum debates around the June-2016 Brexit vote — and the audit reads their disagreement as information.

4a · The trajectory¶

In [9]:
traj = pcd.track(asylum, ['illegal', 'criminal']).over_time(freq='Q', time_col='date')
traj.plot().properties(width=640, height=300, title="Quarterly share — 'illegal' & 'criminal' in asylum debates")
Out[9]:

4b · Five detectors, five readings¶

In [10]:
cps = list(traj.changepoints(target='illegal')['period'])
bo = traj.changepoints_online(target='illegal', hazard=0.02, mu_0=0.0, beta_0=0.0001)
nb = len(traj.burstiness(target='illegal', s=2.0, gamma=1.0).bursts)
its = traj.interrupted_time_series(event_date='2016', target='illegal')
lc = its[its['term'] == 'level_change'].iloc[0]
ba = pcd.compare.before_after(asylum, event_date='2016-01-01', time_col='date').keyness(min_count=5)
shifted = [t for t in ba.table.head(10)['term'] if t not in STOP][:5]
print('changepoints (PELT)      :', [str(c) for c in cps] or 'none')
print('online BOCPD             :', len(bo.detected_changepoints(threshold=3)), 'changepoint(s)')
print('burstiness (Kleinberg)   :', nb, 'burst period(s)')
print(f'interrupted TS @2016     : level {lc["coef"]:+.5f}  p={lc["p_value"]:.3f}  '
      f'({"SIGNIFICANT" if lc["p_value"]<0.05 else "n.s."})')
print('before/after-2016 keyness:', shifted)

4d · Forecast — where is each trajectory heading?¶

In [12]:
traj.forecast(horizon=4, level=0.95).plot().properties(width=640, height=300,
    title='ETS forecast with 95% prediction band')
Out[12]:

What the audit added — the disagreement is the finding. A data-driven break-finder (PELT) flags 2020 (small-boats, COVID), not 2016: left to search, it returns the sharpest step, not your hypothesis. But the instruments that test a date you pre-specified — ITS and the BSTS causal_impact — both find a significant drop at Brexit-2016, and before/after-keyness names the new vocabulary (safe routes, Rwanda, UKBA). That is the placebo logic in miniature: an effect that survives only at the committed anchor is far harder to dismiss as an artifact of the machinery. Choose by what you know — a registered date → ITS/causal_impact; no prior date → changepoints/BOCPD; concentration → burstiness; which words moved → before/after keyness; where it is heading → forecast.

5. When terms compete — which one wins, and when did leadership cross?¶

Some changes are not one term moving but a relay: an old term declining as a new one is adopted, sometimes via a short-lived bridge. The instrument fits a structured model and dates the crossover — which the audit then cross-checks against an independently documented cause (here the AP Stylebook and the historical record), rather than reading causation off the curve.

In [13]:
import analyze_succession as succ
display(succ.summary_frame(['race']))
Image('../figures/succession_race.png')
domain term role t0 share_start share_end crossovers
0 race Negro decline ↓ NaN 0.97 0.13 1992
1 race Afro-American transient/bridge ↑↓ NaN 0.01 0.01 1992
2 race African American clean adoption ↑ 1990.0 0.01 0.81 1992
3 race person of color emerging ↑ 2019.0 0.00 0.05 1992
Out[13]:

What the audit added. A succession is structured change — decline → (optional bridge) → logistic adoption, with a datable crossover that lines up with an independently documented cause at a realistic lag. The registered prediction (the new term overtakes the old) comes with a stated falsifier (it never does within the window). The audit's honesty extends to its own pipeline: the bridge terms (Afro-American here) were discovered in the analysis, not predicted — and the discipline is to say so plainly, and to cross-check each crossover against the historical record rather than dress a discovery as a forecast.

6. Real directional change, or just noise? — and the honesty that cuts in our favour¶

Given an adopted term's rising share: is the rise selection, or could drift produce it? We borrowed four tests from other fields — and the audit's rule is to report which failed. This is where the discipline pays its most distinctive dividend: a method that does not transfer is itself a finding, not an embarrassment to hide.

Method (home field) Verdict on noisy news counts
Diffusion S-curve (innovation studies) ✅ clean — adoptions fit logistics (R² 0.91–1.00); event spikes correctly rejected
Frequency Increment Test (population genetics) ⚠️ under-detects — too conservative here
Kalman state-space (weather / data assimilation) ⚠️ smoothing valid; the trend-test over-detects (spurious regression)
PK/PD impulse-decay (toxicology) ❌ falsified — words don't "clear" like a drug
In [14]:
display(Image('../figures/s_curves.png'))
display(Image('../figures/kalman_smoothing.png'))

What the audit added. No single statistic settles selection-vs-drift on noisy counts — the genetics test under-detects, the weather test over-detects, the toxicology model is outright falsified (words, unlike drugs, do not "clear"). The defensible answer is converging evidence: a clean logistic fit and a documented cause and the concentration dynamics. And an instrument earns trust by what it refuses to fit — the logistic correctly rejecting the 1992 family-values spike is the point, not a footnote.

7. Did the meaning change — and are we even measuring the right sense?¶

Frequency methods are blind to meaning: a word can hold its rate while its sense shifts. But there is a deeper hazard, and it is the paper's central finding — a single-token search silently measures the corpus's dominant sense, not the analyst's intended one, and which sense it returns is a property of the corpus, not the token (it flips between PubMed and Wikipedia). The audit's polysemy safeguard is to quantify sense composition for every query term and watch it over time, validated against an unsupervised second opinion. Four complementary views: three on the framing of immigrant (real SBERT embeddings), and sense_drift tracking CBD/cannabidiol's sense distribution across PubMed.

7d · sense_drift — the sense distribution of CBD shifting (PubMed, null-calibrated)¶

In [18]:
pdf = pd.read_parquet('../data/cbd_pubmed_abstracts.parquet')
X = np.load('../data/cbd_pubmed_embeddings.npy')
pdf = pdf.assign(year=pd.to_numeric(pdf['year'], errors='coerce'))
keep = pdf['year'].notna() & (pdf['year'] <= 2024)
pdf2 = pdf[keep].reset_index(drop=True); pdf2['year'] = pdf2['year'].astype(int)
drift = pcd.sense_drift(pdf2, X[keep.to_numpy()], time_col='year',
                        reference=list(range(2000, 2010)), k=4, n_permutations=25)
print(drift.summary())
print(f'change type: {drift.change_type}  |  permutation p = {drift.p_value:.3f}')
drift.plot()

Sense drift detected from 2010 (15 period(s) flagged); change type: broadening (margin density 0.267, JSD 0.096). Permutation p=0.038. Distinctive terms: dravet, impacts, nanoparticles, lennox-gastaut, covid-, legalization, clobazam, vaping.

7e · The polysemy trap, live — when "CBD" meant Central Business District¶

Everything above measured meaning. The safeguard's blunter purpose is to catch a query that measures the wrong sense entirely — and "CBD" is the cautionary tale most readers will recognize. In academic PubMed (§7d) it means cannabidiol throughout. On Twitter in 2011 it overwhelmingly meant Central Business District — Adelaide job ads, real-estate listings ("great central CBD location"). Cannabidiol was 3% of "CBD" tweets. The senses only crossed around 2015.

In [19]:
import re
tw = pd.read_parquet('../data/cbd_tweets_sample.parquet')
DISTRICT = (r'business district|central business|\bcbd location|office|lease|apartment|\bjob'
            r'|\brates\b|melbourne|sydney|adelaide|brisbane|auckland|perth|downtown|parking'
            r'|for (rent|lease|sale)')
CANNABIS = (r'\boil\b|hemp|cannabis|cannabidiol|marijuana|\bweed\b|\bthc\b|anxiety|gummies'
            r'|tincture|vape|wellness|\bpain\b|\bdose|\bmg\b')
def _sense(s):
    if re.search(CANNABIS, s): return 'cannabidiol'
    if re.search(DISTRICT, s): return 'business_district'
    return 'unclear/other'
tw['sense'] = tw['text'].str.lower().map(_sense)
pct = tw.groupby(['year','sense']).size().unstack(fill_value=0)
pct = (pct.div(pct.sum(1), axis=0)*100).round(0).astype(int)
print('Keyword sense estimate — % of each year\'s "CBD" tweets:')
print(pct[['business_district','cannabidiol','unclear/other']].to_string())

# Corroborate the keyword heuristic with the embedding instrument: senses fit
# on the district-dominated 2011-2014 window, drift monitored forward.
Xt = np.load('../data/cbd_tweets_sample_embeddings.npy')

                        k=4, n_permutations=25)

Sense drift detected from 2015 (7 period(s) flagged); change type: broadening (margin density 0.084, JSD 0.111). Permutation p=0.038. Distinctive terms: nytimes, foxnews, cannabiscommunity, ihub, stockposts, latimes, newyork, topical.

What the audit added — and the safeguard's whole point. The four semantic views answer different questions about meaning (magnitude · which neighbours · trajectory · sense breakdown). But §7e is the safeguard's reason to exist. Two independent instruments agree — the keyword estimate and the embedding sense_drift both put the flip at ~2015 (sense_drift: broadening, p≈0.04) — that on Twitter "CBD" meant Central Business District before it meant cannabidiol. This is the paper's central claim made concrete: the dominant sense of a token is a property of the corpus, not the token, and here it flips within one corpus over time. PubMed's "CBD" is cannabidiol throughout; Twitter's was real estate until 2015. A study that skipped the safeguard and counted "CBD" tweets as cannabis discourse would, in its early years, have been measuring Adelaide job ads — the most basic corpus operation, silently invalid.

8. Beyond English — is Croatian/Serbian one language or several?¶

A famous, politically charged question: after Yugoslavia broke up, are Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian one language or separate ones? keyness (the word-distinguishing tool from §1) becomes the probe. We run it blind on the same news articles written in both Croatian and Serbian (the SETIMES corpus), so any difference it finds is purely a difference between the two standards — not the topic. Two registered wolves: 🐺A separate languages (deep, pervasive differences) vs 🐺B one language, two standards (linguists' term: "pluricentric" — lots of shared words, a few systematic markers). English glosses are in quotes in the figure and below.

In [23]:
import re, statistics
hr = [l.strip() for l in open('../data/bcs/SETIMES.hr-sr.hr', encoding='utf-8').read().splitlines()[:15000]]
sr = [l.strip() for l in open('../data/bcs/SETIMES.hr-sr.sr', encoding='utf-8').read().splitlines()[:15000]]
_t = lambda s: re.findall(r'[a-zšđčćž]+', s.lower())
overlap = statistics.mean((lambda A, B: len(A & B) / len(A | B) if A | B else 0)(set(_t(a)), set(_t(b)))
                          for a, b in zip(hr, sr))
bc = pcd.Corpus(pd.DataFrame({'text': hr + sr, 'lang': ['hr'] * len(hr) + ['sr'] * len(sr)}), text_col='text')
KB = pcd.compare(bc.slice(lang='hr'), bc.slice(lang='sr')).keyness(min_count=15)
print(f'per-sentence token overlap (Croatian vs Serbian): {overlap:.2f}')
print('most Croatian-distinctive:', ', '.join(KB.table[KB.table.log_ratio > 0].head(8)['term']))
print('most Serbian-distinctive :', ', '.join(KB.table[KB.table.log_ratio < 0].sort_values('g2').head(8)['term']))
# a second tool that fits parallel data: size-fair diversity (does purism/morphology
# make one variety lexically richer on *identical* content?)
from pycorpdiff.lexical import hill_numbers, rarefaction
vh, vs = bc.slice(lang='hr').vocab().values, bc.slice(lang='sr').vocab().values
nn = min(int(vh.sum()), int(vs.sum()))
print(f'\nlexical diversity on identical content (rarefied @ {nn:,} tokens):')
print(f'  Croatian: {rarefaction(vh, nn):.0f} types   Serbian: {rarefaction(vs, nn):.0f} types')

Out[23]:

What the audit found — in plain English. Run blind, keyness rediscovers exactly the differences linguists have documented for a century. They come in three flavours:

  • One grammar word, da (≈ "that") — the single biggest difference: Serbian says "I want that I go" where Croatian says "I want to go."
  • Spelling of the same words — predsjednik vs predsednik (both "president"), prije vs pre (both "before"): a regular sound swap, like British "colour" vs American "color."
  • A few everyday word pairs — "with," "also," "during," "euro," "million" each have a separate Croatian and Serbian form.

That an instrument recovers documented linguistics with no prior knowledge is the validation — you can then trust it where the answer isn't known. And it adjudicates the two wolves honestly: the standards share about half their words sentence-for-sentence, and the differences boil down to a few regular rules (≈286 effective markers — real and systematic, but nowhere near enough to read as unrelated languages). So it behaves like one language with two standards, not two separate languages — stated as a measurement, not a political verdict.

A second tool — size-fair diversity — adds a wrinkle: on identical content, Croatian uses a few percent more distinct words (≈71k vs 69k), a small but consistent edge from its grammar and word-purism. (What this snapshot can't show is how the standards drift apart over time — the content is identical and there are no dates. That "drift" question needs different data, which is exactly why §9 turns to Turkish.)

9. Does drift travel to another language? — the Turkish reform as a 100-year succession¶

The instruments are language-agnostic; the harder question is whether drift is too. The cleanest test is a deliberate one. After the Türk Dil Kurumu (Turkish Language Association, 1932), the state systematically replaced Ottoman/Arabic-Persian words with Turkic neologisms. We track four pairs through the Official Gazette + parliamentary records (Turkronicles, decade-separated 1-gram frequencies, 1920–2024), sum inflected forms (Turkish is suffixing), and fit diffusion S-curves — the §5 succession read-out and the §6 S-curve, on an agglutinative non-English language. Measure-three-times: contaminated pairs (millet→ulus, where milletvekili=MP and uluslararası=international swamp the signal) were checked in the data and dropped before fitting.

In [22]:

for _dec in _D:

What the audit found. A flawless deliberate succession: all four Turkic forms rise from ~0% (1920) to ~99% (by ~1970) as clean logistic S-curves (R² 0.98–1.00), with 50%-crossovers in 1936–1948 — right after the 1932 reform, and in the order you'd expect (education first: teacher/school ≈1936–37; student/airplane ≈1946–48). The diffusion-S-curve (§6) and succession read-out (§5) transfer intact to a morphologically rich non-English language — and this is a rare case where the cause (a dated state policy) is documented, not inferred. The agglutination is handled by prefix-summing each root with its consonant-mutation variants (mektep/mekteb, uçak/uçağ); the contaminated pairs were dropped after looking at the data, not guessed. Drift travels.

One honest caveat — the register. This corpus is official/governmental (the Official Gazette + parliament), exactly where a state-driven reform is adopted first and most completely; everyday spoken Turkish lagged the curve. The succession is real and the dating is sound, but its speed reflects the register where the policy bit hardest — the same register caution that applies to the edited-prose limits elsewhere in this notebook.

What the pattern buys¶

Seven instruments, one discipline. Step back, and the same moves recur regardless of the tool:

  • Pick the method by the question — not the question by the method you like.
  • Control the obvious confound before you claim — year (matching, §1), size (rarefaction, §2), chance (the permutation null, §1), a manufactured time-series effect (the placebo/anchor logic, §4), in-sample optimism (the sense-drift null, §7).
  • Prefer converging evidence to any single statistic (§3, §6): a result that survives a clean fit and a documented cause and an orthogonal method is worth more than one small p-value.
  • Report the negatives — the failed transfer (§6), the detector that disagrees (§4), the prediction that misses its falsifier. The honesty cuts in our favour: a scoreboard that includes designed-to-fail predictions, which fail, is the one a sceptic believes.
  • Guard the query itself (§7) — because the most basic operation, searching a token, is the one most quietly invalid.

The pattern is method-agnostic. What it buys is not certainty but auditability: it turns a corpus narrative into a claim someone who distrusts you can check.
